## Learning Objectives

1. Understand the meaning of a correlation
2. Be able to quantify correlations, uncertainty in them, and test the null hypothesis of zero correlation
3. Identify racist and colonial roots of naming conventions, and what to do about it
3. Recognize the assumptions of correlation tests, and what to do when assumptions are violated
4. Interpret correlation results with care

## The meaning of a correlation

*When one variable goes up, the other goes up*

...or...

*When one variable goes up, the other goes down*

## The meaning of a correlation

More fancy sounding:

*How well can we predict one variable from another?*

## How do we quantify correlation?

```{r corr-whiteboard-helpers}
#| include: false

# colors for quadrants where the product of deviations is + (green) or - (blue)
pos_col <- "#51B293"
neg_col <- "#768FF5"

# simulate n points whose sample correlation is exactly r
set.seed(123)

n_pnts <- 12

pos_df <- data.frame(X = scale(rnorm(n_pnts))) |> 
    mutate(Y = X + rnorm(n_pnts, 0, 0.4))
neg_df <- mutate(pos_df, Y = -1 * Y)

set.seed(1)
zero_df <- mutate(pos_df, Y = scale(rnorm(n_pnts)))


# helper function to make quadrant plots
dev_plot <- function(df) {
    xbar <- mean(df$X)
    ybar <- mean(df$Y)
    dx <- diff(range(df$X))
    dy <- diff(range(df$Y))
    pad <- 0.4
    xl <- c(min(df$X) - pad * dx, max(df$X) + pad * dx)
    yl <- c(min(df$Y) - pad * dy, max(df$Y) + pad * dy)
    
    p <- ggplot(df, aes(X, Y))
    
    p <- p +
        annotate("rect", xmin = xbar, xmax = xl[2], ymin = ybar, ymax = yl[2],
                 fill = pos_col, alpha = 0.25) +
        annotate("rect", xmin = xl[1], xmax = xbar, ymin = ybar, ymax = yl[2],
                 fill = neg_col, alpha = 0.25) +
        annotate("rect", xmin = xl[1], xmax = xbar, ymin = yl[1], ymax = ybar,
                 fill = pos_col, alpha = 0.25) +
        annotate("rect", xmin = xbar, xmax = xl[2], ymin = yl[1], ymax = ybar,
                 fill = neg_col, alpha = 0.25)
    
    
    p <- p +
        geom_hline(yintercept = ybar, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_vline(xintercept = xbar, linetype = "dashed") +
        geom_point(size = 4) +
        annotate("point", x = xbar, y = ybar, shape = 3, size = 6, stroke = 1.5)
    
    
    ar <- arrow(length = unit(0.12, "in"), type = "closed")
    p <- p +
        annotate("segment", x = max(df$X) + 0.06 * dx, xend = xl[2] - 0.03 * dx,
                 y = ybar, yend = ybar, arrow = ar, linewidth = 1.2) +
        annotate("segment", x = min(df$X) - 0.06 * dx, xend = xl[1] + 0.03 * dx,
                 y = ybar, yend = ybar, arrow = ar, linewidth = 1.2) +
        annotate("segment", x = xbar, xend = xbar,
                 y = max(df$Y) + 0.06 * dy, yend = yl[2] - 0.03 * dy,
                 arrow = ar, linewidth = 1.2) +
        annotate("segment", x = xbar, xend = xbar,
                 y = min(df$Y) - 0.06 * dy, yend = yl[1] + 0.03 * dy,
                 arrow = ar, linewidth = 1.2) +
        annotate("text",
                 x = c(mean(c(max(df$X), xl[2])), mean(c(min(df$X), xl[1])),
                       xbar + 0.04 * dx, xbar + 0.04 * dx),
                 y = c(ybar + 0.07 * dy, ybar + 0.07 * dy,
                       mean(c(max(df$Y), yl[2])), mean(c(min(df$Y), yl[1]))),
                 label = c("+", "-", "+", "-"),
                 hjust = c(0.5, 0.5, 0, 0), vjust = c(0, 0, 0.5, 0.5),
                 size = 12, fontface = "bold")
    
    
    
    qx <- 0.02 * diff(xl)
    qy <- 0.02 * diff(yl)
    p <- p +
        annotate("text",
                 x = c(xl[2] - qx, xl[1] + qx, xl[1] + qx, xl[2] - qx),
                 y = c(yl[2] - qy, yl[2] - qy, yl[1] + qy, yl[1] + qy),
                 label = c("(+)(+)", "(-)(+)", "(-)(-)", "(+)(-)"),
                 hjust = c(1, 0, 0, 1), vjust = c(1, 1, 0, 0),
                 size = 6, color = "grey20")
    
    
    p +
        scale_x_continuous(breaks = xbar, labels = expression(bar(X))) +
        scale_y_continuous(breaks = ybar, labels = expression(bar(Y))) +
        coord_cartesian(xlim = xl, ylim = yl, expand = FALSE) +
        xlab(expression(italic(X))) +
        ylab(expression(italic(Y))) +
        theme_cowplot() +
        theme(
            axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
            axis.title = element_text(size = 24)
        )
}

# the same data on two different scales (0 to 1 and 0 to 100)
rescale01 <- function(v) 0.05 + 0.9 * (v - min(v)) / (max(v) - min(v))
scale_df_1 <- data.frame(X = rescale01(pos_df$X), Y = rescale01(pos_df$Y))
scale_df_100 <- 100 * scale_df_1

scale_plot <- function(df, top) {
    ggplot(df, aes(X, Y)) +
        geom_point(color = "tomato", size = 4) +
        scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, top), breaks = c(0, top)) +
        scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, top), breaks = c(0, top)) +
        xlab(expression(italic(X))) +
        ylab(expression(italic(Y))) +
        theme_cowplot() +
        theme(
            axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
            axis.title = element_text(size = 24)
        )
}
```

## [Positive]{.alert} correlation

Deviations from the means, $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: "5in"

dev_plot(pos_df)
```

::: {.fragment}
[+]{.alert} deviation of $Y$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ [+]{.alert} deviation of $X$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[−]{.alert} deviation of $Y$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ [−]{.alert} deviation of $X$
:::

## [Covariance]{.alert} and [variance]{.alert}

[Covariance]{.alert} of $X$ and $Y$

$$
\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})
$$

::: {.fragment}
[Variance]{.alert} of $Y$

$$
\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2
$$
:::

## Variance is the covariance of a variable with itself

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Variance of } Y &= \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2 \\
&= \frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \overline{Y})(Y_i - \overline{Y})
\end{aligned}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Compare to the covariance of $X$ and $Y$

$$
\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})
$$
:::



## Covariance captures deviations in the [same direction]{.alert}

::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "4.4in"

dev_plot(pos_df)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Each point contributes $(X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})$

::: {.incremental}
- upper right: $(+)(+) = +$
- lower left: $(-)(-) = +$
:::

::: {.fragment}
All positive contributions, so the sum and the covariance are [positive]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

## [Negative]{.alert} correlation

Deviations from the means, $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: "5in"

dev_plot(neg_df)
```

::: {.fragment}
[+]{.alert} deviation of $Y$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ [−]{.alert} deviation of $X$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[−]{.alert} deviation of $Y$ $\Longleftrightarrow$ [+]{.alert} deviation of $X$
:::

## Covariance captures deviations in [opposite directions]{.alert}

::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "4.4in"

dev_plot(neg_df)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Each point contributes $(X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})$

::: {.incremental}
- upper left: $(-)(+) = -$
- lower right: $(+)(-) = -$
:::

::: {.fragment}
All negative contributions, so the sum and the covariance are [negative]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

## [No]{.alert} correlation

Deviations from the means, $\overline{X}$ and $\overline{Y}$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.3
#| out-width: "5in"

dev_plot(zero_df)
```

::: {.fragment}
[+/−]{.alert} deviation of $Y$ goes with [+/−]{.alert} deviation of $X$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Knowing the direction of the deviation in $X$ tells us nothing about the direction in $Y$
:::

## Covariance captures [no consistent direction]{.alert}

::: {.columns style="align-items: center;"}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| out-width: "4.4in"

dev_plot(zero_df)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
Each point contributes $(X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})$

::: {.incremental}
- $(+)(+) = +$
- $(-)(-) = +$
- $(-)(+) = -$
- $(+)(-) = -$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Positive and negative contributions cancel, so the covariance is [zero]{.alert}
:::
:::
:::

## Covariance depends on the scale of the data

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "3.8in"

scale_plot(scale_df_1, 1)
```

::: {.fragment style="text-align: center;"}
covariance = `r signif(cov(scale_df_1$X, scale_df_1$Y), 2)`
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "3.8in"

scale_plot(scale_df_100, 100)
```

::: {.fragment style="text-align: center;"}
covariance = `r signif(cov(scale_df_100$X, scale_df_100$Y), 2)`
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align: center;"}
[Scale should not matter!]{.alert} We want the same test statistic for both
:::

## [Standardize]{.alert} the covariance

Divide by the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y$ to get the [correlation coefficient]{.alert}

$$
r = \frac{\text{covariance}}{\text{SD}_X \, \text{SD}_Y}
$$

::: {.fragment}
which is bounded

$$
-1 \le r \le 1
$$
:::

## [Standardize]{.alert} the covariance

::: {style="font-size: 0.65em;"}
$$
r = \frac{\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (X_i - \overline{X})^2} \sqrt{\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2}}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
The $\frac{1}{n - 1}$ terms cancel

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
$$
r = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (X_i - \overline{X})(Y_i - \overline{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (X_i - \overline{X})^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i = 1}^{n} (Y_i - \overline{Y})^2}}
$$
:::
:::




## How do we quantify correlation?

Sample correlation coefficient

$$
r = \frac{\sum_i (X_i - \overline{X}) (Y_i - \overline{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (X_i - \overline{X}) ^ 2 \sum_i (Y_i - \overline{Y}) ^ 2}}
$$

is an estimate of population correlation coefficient

$$
\rho = \frac{\sum_i (X_i - \mu_X) (Y_i - \mu_Y)}{\sqrt{\sum_i (X_i - \mu_X) ^ 2 \sum_i (Y_i - \mu_Y) ^ 2}}
$$

## How do we quantify correlation?

The correlation coefficient is bound between -1 and 1

- -1 is perfect negative correlation
- 0 is total lack of correlation
- 1 is perfect positive correlation

## Examples of population $\rho$ versus estimated sample $r$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| out-width: "7in"

set.seed(20210420)
df <- c(-0.9, 0, 0.5, 0.9) |>
    map_dfr(~ {
        ret <- MASS::mvrnorm(25, rep(0, 2), matrix(c(1, .x, .x, 1), ncol = 2)) |>
            as_tibble(.name_repair = NULL) |>
            rename(X = V1, Y = V2) |>
            mutate(rho = .x)
        ret$r <- cor(ret$X, ret$Y)
        ret
    }) |>
    mutate(label = str_c("list(rho==", rho, ",~italic(r)==", round(r, 2), ")"))

ggplot(df, aes(X, Y, label = label)) +
    facet_wrap(label ~ ., nrow = 2, labeller = label_parsed) +
    geom_point(color = "tomato", size = 4) +
    xlab(expression(italic(X))) +
    ylab(expression(italic(Y))) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 24),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 24)
    )
```

## Quantifying uncertanty of correlation estimates

Looking at the equation for estimated correlation:

$$
r = \frac{\sum_i (X_i - \overline{X}) (Y_i - \overline{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (X_i - \overline{X}) ^ 2 \sum_i (Y_i - \overline{Y}) ^ 2}}
$$

::: {.pause-think}

::: {.r-stack}

:::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index="0"}
We see a big summation in the numerator. What distribution do we expect for summations?
::::

:::: {.fragment fragment-index="0"}
We see a big summation in the numerator. What distribution do we expect for summations? A ***normal distribution!***
::::

:::

:::




## Quantifying uncertanty of correlation estimates

Because we are again *estimating* the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $r$, we have to use a *t* distribution

## Null hypothesis testing with correlations

1. State null and alternative hypotheses
2. Calculate test statistic
2. Identify null distribution
3. Calculate $P$-value
4. Decide:
    - Reject null
    - Fail to reject null

## 1. State null and alternative hypotheses

$H_0$ the true population correlation is $\rho = 0$ (most common null)

$H_A$ the true population correlation is not 0

## 2. Calculate test statistic

$$
r = \frac{\sum_i (X_i - \overline{X}) (Y_i - \overline{Y})}{\sqrt{\sum_i (X_i - \overline{X}) ^ 2 \sum_i (Y_i - \overline{Y}) ^ 2}}
$$
Or in *R*:

```{r}
#| echo: true

head(hi_insect, n = 3)

cor(hi_insect$clade_age, hi_insect$clade_richness)
```

## 3. Identify null distribution

We figured out it's a *t*.

degrees of freedom = $n - 1 - (\text{number of parameters estimated})$

so $df = n - 1 - 1$

We could use `pt`, but instead...

## 4. Calculate $P$-value

```{r}
#| echo: true

cor.test(hi_insect$clade_age, hi_insect$clade_richness)
```

## 5. Decide

Because $P = 0.0251$ is less than $\alpha = 0.05$ we reject the null

## Quantifying uncertanty of correlation estimates

We also get the 95% confidence interval from `cor.test`

```{r}
cor.test(hi_insect$clade_age, hi_insect$clade_richness)
```

Again, this comes from the fact that we can assume correlation estimates have a *t* distribution


## Assumptions of correlation tests

1. Random sample
2. $X$ is normal with equal variance for all values of $Y$
3. $Y$ is normal with equal variance for all values of $X$

## What to do when assumptions are violated

- transform (e.g. log transformation)
- rank correlation

## What to do when assumptions are violated: rank correlation

The rank-based test for correlation works by:

1. Ranking all $X$ values
2. Ranking all $Y$ values
3. Calculating $r^2$ for the ranks
4. Testing $r^2$ against $H_0$ of no association from the Spearman distribution

## What to do when assumptions are violated: rank correlation

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false

cor.test(hi_insect$clade_age, hi_insect$clade_richness,
         method = "spearman")
```

## Suprise suprise: Spearman was an asshole too

Obsessed with finding "race"-based differences in "intellegence"

*Deconstructing intellectual memorials will take a lot of community pressure on those who gatekeep statistics*

## Interpret correlation results with care

Correlation measures *linear* association, you can have perfect *non*-linear association with low correlation

```{r}
set.seed(20210420)
df <- tibble(
    X = runif(25, -2, 3),
    Y = -1 + X + 2 * X ^ 2
)
```

In this figure, $r = `r round(cor(df$X, df$Y), 2)`$

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
#| out-width: "6in"

ggplot(df, aes(X, Y)) +
    geom_point(color = "tomato", size = 4) +
    xlab(expression(italic(X))) +
    ylab(expression(italic(Y))) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 24)
    )
```

## Interpret correlation results with care

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "7in"

anscombe_tidy <- anscombe |>
    mutate(observation = seq_len(n())) |>
    pivot_longer(-observation) |>
    separate(name, c("variable", "set"), 1, convert = TRUE) |>
    mutate(set = LETTERS[seq_len(4)][set]) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = "variable", values_from = "value")

ggplot(anscombe_tidy, aes(x, y, color = set)) +
    facet_wrap(vars(set)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", show.legend = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE,
                se = FALSE,
                size = 2, lineend = "round") +
    geom_point(size = 5, alpha = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 20)) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 20)) +
    coord_equal() +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(
        axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 20)
    )
```

## Interpret correlation results with care

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
[Correlation is not causation]{.alert}
:::

## *Correlation is not causation*: the case of lucky socks

Seems like when I wear my lucky socks, good things happen

```{r}
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3
#| out-width: "9in"

set.seed(123)
x <- MASS::mvrnorm(50, c(0, 0), matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), nrow = 2))
x[x >= 0] <- 1
x[x < 1] <- 0

lucky <- cbind(1:nrow(x), x)
lucky <- rbind(lucky[, 1:2], lucky[, c(1, 3)])
lucky <- as.data.frame(lucky)
names(lucky) <- c("day", "event")
lucky$type <- rep(c("I wore\nmy lucky socks", "Something\ngood happened"),
                  each = nrow(x))

lucky <- lucky[lucky$event > 0, ]

ggplot(lucky, aes(x = day, y = event, color = type)) +
    geom_vline(aes(xintercept = day, color = type), linewidth = 1) +
    facet_grid(rows = vars(type)) +
    theme_cowplot() +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          axis.text = element_blank(),
          axis.ticks.length = unit(0, "in"),
          axis.line = element_blank()) +
    xlab("time") +
    ylab("")
```

*We don't have a plausible mechanism where socks can affect the world*

*And I have done no experiment to assess causation*

## But *correlation is expected when there* **is** *causation*: the case of climate change

More $\text{CO}_2$, more hot

![](/img/cenozoic_co2.png){width="50%" fig-align="center"}

We **do** have a plausible mechanism (absorbtion and re-radiation of heat by greenhouse gasses) which is based on experimentally-derived knowledge

We can also build *models* based on this plausible mechanism and show that they accurately predict past and present climate
